 1                                     SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
 2   I.     INTRODUCTION
 3          Defendant Apple’s App Store is the only viable means to make iOS-based mobile software
 4   applications, or “apps,” available to consumers. Plaintiff Musi owns and operates the Musi app, a
 5   popular iOS app that is Musi’s sole source of revenue. On September 24, 2024, Apple abruptly
 6   removed the Musi app from the App Store. While Apple is permitted under its Developer Agreement
 7   to “cease marketing, offering, and allowing download by end-users” of apps that Apple “reasonably
 8   believes, based [on] human and/or systematic review,” infringe the “intellectual property rights of any
 9   third party” (Declaration of Jennifer A. Golinveaux (“Golinveaux Dec.”), ¶ 2, Ex. A (“Dev. Agmt.”)
10   Schedule 1 § 6.3; see also id. ¶ 3, Ex. B (“Dev. Agmt.”) Schedule 2 § 7.3 & Schedule 3 § 7.3), Apple
11   had no such reasonable belief here, much less a reasonable belief based on a “human and/or systematic
12   review” of the underlying claims that led to the Musi app’s removal.
13          Rather, Apple’s removal of the Musi app was based on a five-word complaint dated July 29,
14   2024 from a complainant identified as “YouTube Legal” (“Complainant”), with no supporting
15   evidence or documentation. Despite Musi’s efforts to contact Complainant to understand the basis for
16   its concerns, Complainant—to this day—has failed to respond or to substantiate its accusations.
17   Worse, Apple knew at the time it removed the Musi app that Complainant had failed to substantiate
18   its claims. Apple’s improper removal of the Musi app has caused—and continues to cause—
19   substantial and irreparable harm to Musi’s business and reputation. Thus, Apple has breached the
20   Developer Agreement and the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
21          By removing the Musi app from its only viable distribution platform, Apple has exiled Musi
22   from its customer base—thereby threatening the company’s survival. Musi is therefore entitled to a
23   preliminary injunction to stop Apple from continuing to breach the Developer Agreement by refusing
24   to list or otherwise making unavailable the Musi app. Apple’s obligations are plain, Musi is likely to
25   prevail on the merits, and the Court may enforce the Developer Agreement to protect Musi from
26   incurring further irreparable harm.
27

 1   II.    RELEVANT FACTUAL BACKGROUND
 2          A.      The App Store
 3          Apple designs, manufactures, and sells mobile computing devices, including “iPhone” branded

 4   smartphones. iPhones are portable, connect wirelessly to the internet, and enjoy advanced computing

 5   capabilities, including internet browsing. See Golinveaux Dec. ¶ 4, Ex. C (“Wired.com Article”). To

 6   function, iPhones rely on Apple’s proprietary mobile operating system called “iOS,” which is pre-

 7   installed on every device. See id. ¶ 5, Ex. D (“Javapoint.com Article”). Users often rely on third-party

 8   iOS apps to fully enjoy their iPhone’s capabilities.

 9          When the iPhone was launched in 2007, Apple initially refused to host third-party iOS apps.

10   Id. ¶ 6, Ex. E (“Guardian Article”). However, Apple changed course the following year and launched

11   the App Store—a dedicated online marketplace that allows users to browse and download third-party

12   apps for iPhone. See id. ¶ 8, Ex. F (“Apple.com 2008 Article”); see also id. ¶ 8, Ex. G (“July 5, 2018

13   Apple.com Article Titled The App Store turns 10”). Today, the App Store hosts nearly two million

14   apps—more than 99.99% of which were developed by third-party developers. Id. ¶ 9, Ex. H

15   (“Caminade & Wartburg Study”) at p.1.

16          The App Store is the only viable means by which iOS apps are distributed to consumers. See

17   id. ¶ 10, Ex. I (“Morton Paper”). As the developer, owner, and operator of the App Store, Apple enjoys

18   singular power to choose which iOS apps are made available on the platform. See id. ¶ 2, Ex. A, Dev.

19   Agmt. §§ 3.2(g), 6.9. Even so, Apple’s power is limited by the terms and conditions enumerated in

20   the Developer Agreement, signed by every third party who wishes to distribute an iOS app for the App

21   Store—including Musi. See id. ¶¶ 2–3, Ex. A & B, Dev. Agreement; Aaron Wojnowski Declaration

22   (“Wojnowski Dec.”), ¶ 5.

23          B.      Apple’s Developer Program License Agreement
24          The Developer Agreement grants third-party developers a limited, personal, non-exclusive,

25   and revocable license to use Apple’s software and services, provided the developer builds and operates

26   its app in compliance with the Developer Agreement’s terms and conditions. Golinveaux Dec. ¶ 2, Ex.

27   A, Dev. Agmt. §§ 1.1, 2.1, 3.2(a). And if a developer wishes to make an iOS app available on the App

28   Store, it must apply for distribution with Apple. Id. ¶ 2, Ex. A, Dev. Agmt. §§ 6.1, 6.9.

 1          To qualify for distribution, the third-party app must comply with the “Documentation and
 2   Program Requirements then in effect as well as with any additional guidelines that Apple may post.”
 3   Id. ¶ 2, Ex. A, Dev, Agmt. § 6.1. Once the app is deemed qualified (i.e., a “Licensed Application”),
 4   the third-party developer must agree to additional conditions enumerated in Schedule 1, Schedule 2,
 5   or Schedule 3 of the Developer Agreement depending on the app’s nature. See id. ¶ 2, Ex. A, Dev.
 6   Agmt. Purpose.
 7          If the third-party app is distributed for free on the App Store, then it is subject to Schedule 1.
 8   Id. ¶ 2, Ex. A, Dev. Agmt. § 7.1. Schedule 1 § 1.2(b) states that the third-party developer must
 9   authorize Apple to “provide hosting services[,] . . . subject to the terms of the Agreement, in order to
10   allow for the storage of, and end-user access to, the Licensed Applications” on the App Store. Id. ¶ 2,
11   Ex. A, Dev. Agmt. Schedule 1 § 1.2(b). And Schedule 1 § 4.1(b) requires the third-party developer to
12   guarantee to Apple that “none of the Licensed Applications . . . violate or infringe any . . . intellectual
13   property or contractual rights of any other person, firm, corporation or other entity.” Id. ¶ 2, Ex. A,
14   Dev. Agmt. Schedule 1 § 4.1(b). If a dispute arises over the content or use of a Licensed Application,
15   the third-party developer must permit Apple to share its contact information with the party filing the
16   dispute and follow Apple’s app dispute process “on a non-exclusive basis and without any party
17   waiving its legal rights.” Id. ¶ 2, Ex. A, Dev. Agmt. § 4.1(g).
18          Relatedly, Schedule 1 § 6.3 states that Apple “reserves the right to cease marketing, offering,
19   and allowing download by end-users of the Licensed Applications at any time, with or without good
20   cause, by providing notice of termination to” the developer. Id. ¶ 2, Ex. A, Dev. Agmt. Schedule 1
21   § 6.3. But Schedule 1 § 6.3 goes on to state:

23          cease allowing download by end-users of some or all of the Licensed Applications, or
            take other interim measures in Apple’s sole discretion, if Apple reasonably believes,
24          based [on] human and/or systematic review, and, including without limitation upon

25          any end-user’s possession and/or use of those Licensed Applications, infringe patent,

 1           C.      The Musi App
 2           Musi is a mobile computing software company founded in Manitoba, Canada. Wojnowski Dec.

 3   ¶ 1. Released in 2013, the Musi app provides users with enhanced functionality to interact with

 4   publicly available content on YouTube’s website through Musi’s augmentative interface. Id. ¶ 2. The

 5   Musi app does not rely on YouTube’s Application Programming Interface (“API”), nor do Musi’s

 6   servers store, process, or transmit YouTube videos. Id. Instead, the Musi app plays or displays content

 7   based on the user’s interactions with YouTube and enhances that experience via Musi’s proprietary

 8   technology. Id.

 9           Musi remains the sole owner and operator of the Musi App, and since its launch, the app has

10   become popular among younger users. See id. ¶ 4. This popularity has allowed Musi to operate

11   continuously for over a decade with a small team headquartered in Manitoba, and, for years, the Musi

12   app has been ranked a top 200 app in the App Store. Id. As Musi’s only product, the Musi app remains

13   its sole revenue source. Id. ¶ 8.

14           D.      Apple’s Unreasonable Removal of the Musi App from the App Store
15                   1.      Musi’s Correspondence with Apple Pre-2024
16           Since at least 2015, Musi has engaged in sporadic dialogue with YouTube. Wojnowski ¶ 6.

17   Throughout, Musi has repeatedly expressed its commitment to offer the Musi app in a way that

18   complies with YouTube’s Terms of Service. Id. Accordingly, whenever YouTube has raised concerns

19   with the Musi app’s functionality, Musi has, in good faith, either (a) adjusted the app’s functionality,

20   or (b) provided details about how the app works and explained why it is fully compliant with

21   YouTube’s Terms of Service. Id. ¶ 7.

22           In April 2021, YouTube’s outside counsel raised several questions regarding the Musi app’s

23   functionality. Declaration of Michael S. Elkin (“Elkin Dec.”) ¶ 2. Musi promptly responded and

24   directly answered each question by substantively describing the Musi app’s functionality; yet

25   YouTube never replied. Id.; Wojnowski Dec. ¶ 7. Instead, in March 2023, YouTube sent a complaint

26   notification to Apple about the Musi app, stating only “YouTube TOS Violations.” Elkin Dec. ¶ 3.

27   Musi, again, promptly responded, only to be met again with YouTube’s silence. Id. Since May 5,

28   2021—when Musi, through outside counsel, substantively described the functionality and addressed

 1   YouTube’s comments—Musi has continued to offer the Musi app on the App Store. Wojnowski Dec.
 2   ¶ 7. Musi has conducted routine updates to the Musi app, but the app has otherwise operated in a
 3   substantially similar manner since that time. Id.
 4                   2.       Musi and Apple’s 2024 Correspondence and the Musi App’s Removal
 5          On August 8, 2024, Apple—via representatives of its App Store—emailed Musi, stating that
 6   it had received a notice from “YouTube Legal” on July 29, 2024, stating “that Claimant believes” the
 7   Musi app “infringes its intellectual property rights. In particular, Claimant believes [the Musi app]
 8   infring[es] its terms of use,” and directed Musi to “see their comments below.” Elkin Dec. ¶ 4, Ex. A
 9   (“Aug. 8, 2024 Apple Email”). The referenced “comments” were five words: “violating YouTube
10   Terms of Service.” Id.
11          Apple’s August 8, 2024 email did not provide any other details about the basis for
12   Complainant’s assertions. Neither the nature of Complainant’s intellectual property nor the specific
13   sections of Complainant’s Terms of Service allegedly violated were referenced. Id. That said, Musi’s
14   outside counsel responded to Apple on August 12, explaining that Complainant’s accusations were
15   “unsubstantiated,” and that Musi had previously contacted Complainant directly to resolve the dispute.
16   Id. ¶ 5, Ex. B (“Aug. 12, 2024 Response”).
17          A month later, on September 6, Complainant emailed Apple again and inaccurately claimed
18   that Musi failed to initiate contact to resolve the dispute. Id. ¶ 6, Ex. B (“Sept. 6, 2024 Complaint”).
19   In doing so, Complainant carbon copied—without explanation—several third parties that have no
20   apparent relation to the matter. See id. In any event, Musi’s outside counsel responded to correct the

13   III.    ARGUMENT: THE COURT SHOULD ISSUE A PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION
14           Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65 provides for the issuance of a preliminary injunction to
15   “preserve the status quo ante litem pending a determination of the action on the merits.” L.A. Mem’l
16   Coliseum Comm’n v. Nat’l Football League, 634 F.2d 1197, 1200 (9th Cir. 198). Musi is entitled to a
17   preliminary injunction if it shows (1) that it is “likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of
18   preliminary relief”; (2) that it is “likely to succeed on the merits”; (3) “that the balance of equities tips
19   in [its] favor”; and (4) “that an injunction is in the public interest.” hiQLabs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp.,
20   31 F.4th 1180, 1188 (9th Cir. 2022) (quoting Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20
21   (2008)). The Ninth Circuit follows a “sliding scale” approach, in which these elements “are balanced,
22   so that a stronger showing of one element may offset a weaker showing of another.” All. for the Wild
23   Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127, 1131–35 (9th Cir. 2011)). Thus, for example, an injunction can
24   issue if there are “serious questions going to the merits” and the balance of hardships “tips sharply in
25   the [movant’s] favor,” provided that Musi shows that “there is a likelihood of irreparable injury and
26   that the injunction is in the public interest.” Id. at 1135.
27           As shown in detail below, Musi satisfies all four elements. First, without preliminary relief,
28   Musi will remain exiled from its customer base and thus, faces extinction. Second, the balance of

 1          However, in Intango, the “reasonable opinion” language in § 7 of Mozilla’s Add-on
 2   Distribution Agreement was not at issue—and for good reason. Unlike Apple’s conduct here, Mozilla
 3   engaged in “extensive” discussions with Intango before blocking and disabling Intango’s add-ons from

 5   named the exact provision of the Add-on Distribution Agreement that it suspected the add-ons were
 6   violating. See id. And on one occasion, Mozilla lifted the block after learning more about their
 7   functionality. See id. Nothing similar happened here. Apple did not engage in any “extensive”
 8   discussions with Musi. To the contrary, Apple ignored Musi’s correspondence, made no attempt to
 9   communicate with Musi to gather details surrounding its position, and removed the Musi app from the
10   App Store without providing any bases for its belief that the app violated Complainant’s intellectual
11   property and/or Terms of Service.
12          Even assuming for the sake of argument that Apple and Complainant engaged in more
13   extensive conversations (without Musi’s involvement or knowledge), such one-sided conversations
14   would not be enough to form a “reasonable belief” that the Musi app infringed Complainant’s
15   intellectual property. The ordinary and popular meaning of “reasonable belief” is one that is “in
16   accordance with reason, fairness, duty or prudence.” See Reasonable, Merriam-Webster.com,
17   https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/reasonable (last visited Oct. 4, 2023). There is nothing
18   “fair” or “prudent” about engaging in a one-sided inquiry where a company’s survival is at stake. And
19   it undoubtedly contradicts Apple’s “dut[ies]” under the Developer Agreement. At a minimum, Musi
20   has shown that there are serious questions as to its claim for breach of contract.
21                  2.      Breach of the Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing
22          Musi also raises a claim for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. This
23   covenant is implied by law in every contract. Thrifty Payless, Inc. v. The Americana at Brand, LLC,
24   218 Cal. App. 4th 1230, 1244 (2013). Under this covenant, “no party to the contract will do anything
25   that would deprive another party” of the contract’s benefits. Miller v. Zurich Am. Ins., 41 Cal. App.
26   5th 247, 257 (2019) (citation omitted). Further, it “requires each party to do everything the contract
27   presupposes the party will do to accomplish the agreement’s purposes.” Thrifty Payless, Inc., 218 Cal.
28   App. 4th at 1244. “Although a breach of the implied covenant . . . is necessarily a breach of contract,
                                                        17
                                      PL.’S MOTION FOR PRELIMINARY INJ.
                                            CASE NO. 5-24-CV-06920

 1   the scope of conduct prohibited by the implied covenant often is pleaded as a separate count.” Miller,
 2   41 Cal. App. 5th at 257. (citation omitted). Thus, a breach of contract may also breach the implied
 3   covenant of good faith and fair dealing where the conduct involves something beyond the breach of
 4   the contractual duty itself. See Congleton v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins., 189 Cal. App. 3d 51, 59 (1987).
 5          To state a claim, Musi must allege: (1) the existence of a contractual relationship; (2) an
 6   implied duty; (3) breach; and (4) causation. See Smith v. San Francisco, 225 Cal. App. 3d 38, 49
 7   (1990). Here, the way in which Apple breached the Developer Agreement separately breaches the
 8   implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
 9          Implicit in its contractual obligation to conduct a “human and/or systematic review” of
10   Claimant’s claims was a duty to execute those obligations in good faith. After all, “[t]he covenant of
11   good faith finds particular application in situations where one party,” like Apple, “is invested with a
12   discretionary power affecting the rights of another,” like Musi. Carma Developers (Cal.) Inc. v.
13   Marathon Dev. Cal., Inc., 2 Cal. 4th 342, 371 (1992). Here, Apple did not in good faith investigate
14   Claimant’s claims. Instead, it accepted Claimant’s unsubstantiated accusations at face value, and—
15   based on that bad faith assumption—destroyed Musi’s business. For these reasons, there are, at a
16   minimum, serious questions as to whether Apple “subjectively lack[ed] belief in the validity of its acts
17   or” whether “its conduct was objectively unreasonable.” Id. Accordingly, Musi is separately entitled
18   to a preliminary injunction on its claim for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair
19   dealing.

11          Having considered Plaintiff Musi Inc. (“Musi”) Motion for Preliminary Injunction (“Motion”)

12   against Defendant Apple Inc. (“Apple”), the Opposition, and Reply papers; the evidence presented in

13   support and in opposition to the Motion; the parties’ oral arguments; and the records on file in this

14   matter; the Court hereby GRANTS the Motion and finds and concludes that:

15          1.        Musi is likely to succeed on the merits of its claim for breach of contract. The evidence

16   establishes a likelihood that Musi will prove that Apple has breached Schedule 1 § 6.3, Schedule 2 §

17   7.3, and Schedule 3 § 7.3 of Apple’s Developer Program License Agreement (“Developer

18   Agreement”) by refusing to list or otherwise making unavailable the Musi mobile software application

19   (“Musi app”) from the Apple App Store.

20          2.        Musi is also likely to succeed on the merits of its claim for breach of the implied

21   covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Musi has adduced sufficient evidence to establish the

22   likelihood of proving that Apple has breached Schedule 1 § 6.3, Schedule 2 § 7.3, and Schedule 3

23   § 7.3 of the Development Agreement in bad faith.

24          3.        Musi has demonstrated that it is likely to suffer immediate and irreparable injury if

25   Apple is not enjoined from continuing to breach Schedule 1 § 6.3, Schedule 2 § 7.3, and Schedule 3 §

26   7.3 of the Developer Agreement by refusing to list or otherwise making unavailable the Musi app from

27   the App Store.

28          4.        The balance of hardships tips sharply in favor of issuing a preliminary injunction.

 1   Without preliminary relief, Musi faces irreparable harm. And with the granting of relief, Apple will

 3          5.      The public interest favors issuing a preliminary injunction. Without preliminary relief,
 4   nearly 2 million third-party iOS developers face uncertainty as to their contractual rights under the
 5   Developer Agreement.
 6          Based on the foregoing findings of fact and conclusions of law, it is hereby ORDERED and
